title: Shabari
hook: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha rose from the fire and pointed the way: Sugriva, and an old woman named Shabari. Did you set one mask down? Day five hundred seventy-eight.

On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world. One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come here one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.
screen: `A HERMITAGE BY LAKE PAMPA.` → `THE TEACHERS ARE GONE.` → `ONE WOMAN WAITS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and her name points to the Shabaras, a forest people. When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks her the questions you'd ask any respected elder. Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Are your vows kept? Is your mind at peace? Then she answers, and here's the first idea. She says, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Second idea: look at who is honoring whom. Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old forest woman of a community many in his world would have looked down on. The text makes no speech about it. It just shows a prince sitting in her hermitage, asking about her inner life, and receiving what she gives him. Third, the story most people know: that Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama, and he ate them gladly. It's one of the most loved scenes in Hindu devotion. But it isn't in Valmiki. It grew in later tellings, in regional Ramayanas, songs and sermons. In Valmiki she simply offers the fruits she gathered. Both are worth knowing: what the old text says, and what centuries of love added to it.
screen: `SHABARI, A WOMAN ASCETIC.` · `MY PRACTICE HAS BORNE FRUIT.` · `A PRINCE IN A FOREST HERMITAGE.` · `THE TASTED BERRIES: A LATER TELLING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture someone who has waited a long time for something good. Maybe it's you. Breathe in, and feel the waiting: not impatient, just steady. Breathe out, and let it be enough to keep the place ready, the way Shabari kept the hermitage and gathered the fruit. You don't need to know when. Just sit, ready. The bell holds the time.
Shabari. The forest ascetic who waited at Matanga's hermitage, and said her practice bore fruit the day Rama came.
Your line: Shabari. Today, give someone the best of what you have, even if it's small and simple. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Shabari is widely loved as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; the berry story is told in many later Ramayanas, songs and sermons, and some temples and festivals honor her.

original.note: Sanskrit śabarī: a woman of the Śabara, a forest people. the name of the ascetic at Matanga's hermitage.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shabari is the woman who tasted the berries.
what it means: in Valmiki she's an ascetic whose long practice is fulfilled by Rama's visit.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 74 calls her a śramaṇī and has her offer gathered fruits; the tasted-berry motif appears in later regional and devotional retellings.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 73–74 (Matanga's hermitage; Shabari welcomes Rama)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering and differ between editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper uses.
'Her name points to the Shabaras, a forest people': standard reading of the name; Valmiki does not dwell on her birth. Confirm wording.
'A community many in his world would have looked down on': interpretive; a Keeper may wish to soften.
